extracted.intended_audience: aspiring creative writers and students considering/participating in the Coursera Wesleyan Creative Writing Specialization
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for completing weekly creative-writing assignments in Wesleyan University's Coursera Creative Writing Specialization (short/micro fiction with peer review and a capstone). Emphasizes word-count constraints, revision, peer-review norms, and technical correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to word count limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Every weekly assignment comes with a word count limit; adhering to the word count limit is paramount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limits increase as the course progresses (examples: 250, 500, 1000). Meeting the limit is a weekly exercise and parallels real-world quotas from agents/editors/publishers. Submissions well over the limit demonstrate lack of effort and may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to edit down without compromising the story
rubrics_metrics.description: After drafting, revise to reduce length while preserving story completeness and impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cutting content effectively is taught in the courses; the author describes repeatedly revising over days to meet counts. The skill is essential when initial drafts exceed the limit but must still feel complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete the assignment within the stated requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure the story is 'complete within the constraints' and that all assignment requirements are checked and satisfied before submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check assignment-specific prompts and any formatting/structural requirements; failing to follow requirements indicates the student did not learn the week's lesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revise extensively / multiple editing passes
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not publish or submit without extensive revisions; thorough editing is an expected part of producing quality writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites Stephen King spending 3–4 months of full-time editing as an example. The author spends several hours across days revising each short/micro story and runs work through tools like Grammarly to catch issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grammar, spelling, and technical correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions should be free (or nearly free) of spelling and grammar errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large numbers of mistakes (example: '43 grammar errors in 600 words') are unacceptable. Use proofreading tools (e.g., Grammarly) and manual revision to correct errors before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and plagiarism-free text
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories must be original; plagiarism is a serious problem that should be detected and avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author observed a peer's submission flagged as plagiarism by Grammarly. Recommends automatic plagiarism checks (e.g., integrate a plagiarism API) to enforce originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration of learning (apply the week's craft lesson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments should show that the student applied what was taught that week (plot techniques, character craft, setting/description, or style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submissions that 'did not show he/she learned anything that week' are grounds for failing; peer reviewers should assess whether lessons were applied, not just quantity of words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional, courteous, and constructive peer reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewing peers, be professional and courteous, and provide constructive criticism that reinforces what you learned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each week requires reviewing three peers. Reviewing others reinforces learning; reviewers should give actionable feedback rather than unhelpful comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer-review process rules: submit before reviewing
rubrics_metrics.description: You must submit your own work before you can review peers' assignments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural rule ensures accountability and encourages sincere participation rather than gaming the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and formatting correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions must have clear structure and correct formatting appropriate for the assignment and genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author called out submissions with 'no structure, no format' as failures. Reviewers should check that plotting, scene structure, and required formatting (e.g., paragraphing, dialogue) are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialogue formatting and conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper dialogue formatting is a distinct technical skill that many students lack and should be taught/applied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests the course should discuss dialogue formatting because many students appear clueless; reviewers/instructors should check correct punctuation and paragraphing for dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement of course policies (recommended)
rubrics_metrics.description: Course staff should enforce word count quotas and limits and take steps to actively moderate forums and submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author recommends enforcing quotas, adding automatic plagiarism testing, and dedicating instructor time to forum engagement to prevent the course from becoming passive income and to raise quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of course peer-review to reinforce learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is part of the learning loop: submit, review peers, and learn by critiquing others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The course requires peer review of three peers per week; the activity is intended to reinforce craft lessons and encourage critical application of techniques learned in the videos and readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of publication/portfolio outcomes (capstone visibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capstone and course outputs should be considered as potential publication or portfolio pieces; the author suggests showcasing winners (e.g., an anthology).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing a digital anthology of capstone winners would motivate higher-quality work and give students real-world exposure; instructors should communicate expectations if work is to be portfolio-ready.
